title: Collage crossing labels classify enriched fixed-end transformations
statement:
Use the universes, quasicategories, coherent functors and transformations of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], the space-valued coherent Hom bifunctor of [lem-coef-infinity-hom-bifunctor-functoriality], the space category of [def-coef-infinity-category-of-spaces], the enriched tensor/cotensor adjunction of [lem-coef-enriched-category-tensor-calculus], and the collage of [lem-coef-space-bimodule-collage]. Let $\mathcal V$ be a presentably closed symmetric monoidal infinity-category and $\mathcal E$ a complete $\mathcal V$-category, $S$ a small infinity-category, $v\in\mathcal V$, and $P,Q:S\to U\mathcal E$ coherent diagrams. The enriched composition and units of $\mathcal E$ make $(x,y)\mapsto\mathcal E(x,y)$ a coherent functor $(U\mathcal E)^{\mathrm{op}}\times U\mathcal E\to\mathcal V$ whose actions are precomposition and postcomposition, with all unit and composition simplices; this is part of the assertion. Put $H_v(x,y)=\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal V}(v,\mathcal E(x,y))$, the composite of this functor with the coherent Hom bifunctor of $\mathcal V$ at $v$, and let $C_v=\operatorname{Coll}(H_v)$ with source and target endpoint copies $(U\mathcal E)_0,(U\mathcal E)_1$. Then the mixed fixed-end mapping space in the collage is naturally equivalent to the enriched transformation space:
$$\operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{Fun}(S,C_v)}(P_0,Q_1)\simeq\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal V}\bigl(v,\mathcal E^S(P,Q)\bigr).$$
Under the tensor/cotensor adjunction, the right side is the space of coherent enriched maps $T_v\otimes S_{\mathcal V}\to\mathcal E$ with endpoint diagrams $P$ and $Q$, where $T_v$ is the completion of the free algebroid on two fixed objects and one generating edge labeled by $v$, as in [lem-coef-algebroid-presentability]. The equivalence sends a map to its crossing labels in $H_v(Ps,Qt)$ and sends compatible labels back to the unique mixed-string map. It is natural in $v,S,P,Q$, in coherent maps of endpoint diagrams, and in additional space-valued parameters; it retains every higher coherence simplex.

source.place: §2.3.1 Definition 2.3.1.3 and Remark 2.3.1.4, with the complete-Segal collage presentation; the fixed-end crossing-label equivalence and tensor/cotensor identification are agent-formulated refinements. Read online; archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: Construct the asserted $\mathcal V$-valued Hom functor directly from the algebroid operations; it is not supplied as a theorem by tensor calculus. For endpoint arrows $f:x'\to x$, $g:y\to y'$, represent them by $\mathbf1\to\mathcal E(x',x)$ and $\mathbf1\to\mathcal E(y,y')$. Insert these on the two sides of the middle factor in the three-input composition to obtain $\mathcal E(x,y)\to\mathcal E(x',y')$, $h\mapsto g h f$. An $n$-simplex of $U\mathcal E$ is, by the adjunction between free enrichment and $U$ in tensor calculus applied to $K=\Delta^n$, an enriched functor $(\Delta^n)_{\mathcal V}\to\mathcal E$: its points $\mathbf1\to\mathcal E(x_i,x_j)$ come with their composition simplices in the algebroid. For chains $x_n\to\cdots\to x_0$ and $y_0\to\cdots\to y_n$, so represented, keep the middle factor uncomposed and use the algebroid's operation on each longer string to supply the simplex between the corresponding Hom objects. A face composes adjacent endpoint inputs or removes an extreme input; a degeneracy inserts its unit. Their compatibilities are exactly the operadic composition and inert-restriction compatibilities in the definition of an algebroid. This also treats families: for a space $K$ of endpoint arrows, use the adjoint map $K\otimes\mathbf1\to\mathcal E(x',x)$, and similarly on the right; separate colimit preservation turns their tensor into the family indexed by the product of the parameter spaces. Thus the construction supplies all simplices of a coherent functor $(U\mathcal E)^{\mathrm{op}}\times U\mathcal E\to\mathcal V$. Compose with the coherent Hom functor $\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal V}(v,-)$ to get $H_v$.

source.place: §4.3, algebroid operations; direct marked-middle-slot construction by the agent.

proof.text: Apply the collage lemma with $C=D=U\mathcal E$ and $H=H_v$. Its smallness hypothesis concerns $U\mathcal E$: the enriched category has a small object space, and its underlying mapping spaces are small in the fixed universes of tensor calculus. The smallness of $S$ is used later, not here. Put $A_v\subseteq\operatorname{Fun}(\Delta^1,C_v)$ equal to the full subcategory on mixed arrows, with endpoint evaluation to $U\mathcal E\times U\mathcal E$. Its objects are $(x,y,a)$ with $a\in H_v(x,y)$. For mixed arrows $a:x_0\to y_1$ and $b:x'_0\to y'_1$, the arrow-morphism-square lemma describes a morphism as endpoint arrows $f:x\to x'$, $g:y\to y'$ and a path $b f\simeq g a$ in $H_v(x,y')$. This is the homotopy equalizer of the two maps from the product of endpoint mapping spaces to $H_v(x,y')$. The collage lemma identifies these two maps and their higher actions with enriched precomposition and postcomposition, and its mixed-string presentation specifies their coherent compositions.

source.place: §2.3.1 Definition 2.3.1.3 and Remark 2.3.1.4; coherent square description from the cited arrow-morphism statement.

proof.text: Put $B_v=U\operatorname{Fun}_{\mathcal V}(T_v,\mathcal E)$. Apply the free-enriched-edge square presentation to the complete target $\mathcal E$. It presents its objects by exactly the triples $(x,y,a:v\to\mathcal E(x,y))$ and its morphisms by $(f,g,\gamma:b f\simeq g a)$, with the whole path space and all strings of squares. This result concerns only the single free edge. In particular it makes no assertion about $\mathcal E^S(P,Q)$ or enriched ends. Since $H_v(x,y')=\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal V}(v,\mathcal E(x,y'))$, the endpoint maps $d_0,d_1$ and paths in this presentation are exactly those calculated for $A_v$ in step 2.

source.place: Remark 9.5 and Gepner–Haugseng Remark 4.3.4; agent-formulated free-edge square refinement.

proof.text: Compare the two complete Segal presentations over $U\mathcal E\times U\mathcal E$. Send a triple $(x,y,a)$ of $B_v$ to the mixed arrow labeled by $a$ in $A_v$. On a string of squares keep its two endpoint strings and its paths $b f\simeq g a$, interpreting the latter by the mixed-string presentation of the collage. This defines the comparison on the whole string, including its compatibility simplices; it is not a choice of a homotopy for each commutative square. Conversely read those same labels and paths. Inner faces on both sides paste paths and compose endpoint arrows; outer faces restrict and degeneracies insert identities. Hence these two operations commute with every simplicial operator and are inverse on the coherent presentations. The complete-Segal/quasicategory comparison gives an equivalence $B_v\simeq A_v$ over the endpoint category. This is the endpoint-fibration comparison; no enriched twisted-arrow formula was used to obtain it.

source.place: §2.3.1 correspondence; explicit comparison of square/string presentations by the agent.

proof.text: Take coherent $S$-diagrams in this equivalence and fix the endpoint diagrams to $(P,Q)$. Work with the homotopy fibers on cores, so fixing endpoints includes their specified coherent identifications. The resulting space for $A_v$ is the space of mixed transformations from $P_0$ to $Q_1$ in $\operatorname{Fun}(S,C_v)$: by the definition of internal functor simplicial sets, a diagram of mixed arrows is the same map $S\times\Delta^1\to C_v$, and the same product rearrangement works with every additional simplex parameter. Restriction along $S\times\partial\Delta^1\hookrightarrow S\times\Delta^1$ is an isofibration by the exponentiation lemma. Its strict endpoint fiber computes the categorical pullback and its core computes the homotopy fiber by the isofibration-pullback lemma. All transformations in that fiber are equivalences, since their endpoint components are identities; the componentwise criterion of functor-cone calculus therefore makes it a space. The pinch comparison identifies this fixed-end arrow space with $\operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{Fun}(S,C_v)}(P_0,Q_1)$. Postcomposing diagrams with the inverse equivalences in step 4 and their endpoint-compatible homotopies gives inverse maps on these spaces. Thus the left side of the required equivalence is the fixed-end space of $S$-diagrams in $B_v$.

source.place: Internal-functor product adjunction and fixed-end mapping-space comparison; agent argument after the endpoint-preserving equivalence of step 4.

proof.text:
Apply the cotensor identity of tensor calculus with $\mathcal A=T_v$ and $K=S$:
$$\operatorname{Fun}_{\mathcal V}(T_v,\mathcal E)^S\simeq\operatorname{Fun}_{\mathcal V}(T_v,\mathcal E^S).$$
Its underlying category on the left is $\operatorname{Fun}(S,B_v)$ by the coherent cotensor identification. Evaluation at the two distinguished objects of $T_v$ corresponds under this identity to the two endpoint $S$-diagrams, so its fiber fixes the objects $P,Q$ in $\mathcal E^S$. The free-algebroid universal property identifies the space of enriched functors $F_v\to\mathcal E^S$ with these endpoints with $\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal V}(v,\mathcal E^S(P,Q))$. Because $\mathcal E^S$ is complete, restriction along $F_v\to LF_v=T_v$ is an equivalence on these functor spaces; locality and the completion unit in the completion lemma justify this restriction. Therefore the fixed-end space of step 5 is exactly the claimed right side. Uncurrying also identifies it with enriched maps $T_v\otimes S_{\mathcal V}\to\mathcal E$ having endpoints $P,Q$, proving the additional probe clause.

source.place: Remark 9.5; cotensor/currying identity and completion, with the fixed-end free-graph property from Gepner–Haugseng Remark 4.3.4.

proof.text: The comparison reads mixed labels and its inverse glues their coherent mixed strings, by steps 2–4. The free-edge and cotensor identifications use endpoint evaluation, so the equivalence of steps 5–6 has these same component evaluations. A label at a nonidentity arrow $s\to t$ of $S$ lies in $H_v(Ps,Qt)$; its indexing is the twisted-arrow diagram, not the set of all pairs of objects. We use no formula for an enriched end here. Restriction in $S$, precomposition by a coefficient map $v'\to v$, and coherent maps of endpoint diagrams act on the same labels, paths and strings on both sides. The collage and free-edge presentations commute with these operations and with space parameters, while currying and completion are coherent; the inverse homotopies consequently commute with them as well. For $S=\varnothing$ both fixed-end spaces are contractible (the enriched terminal category has terminal Hom object). For $S=*$ they reduce to $H_v(P,Q)$. For $v=\mathbf1$ the labels are ordinary mapping-space arrows; the comparison is the ordinary coherent transformation comparison.

source.place: Remark 9.5; parameter compatibility in the cited presentations and direct edge-case checks.

proof_origin.place: Repair of the circular enriched-end argument: direct Hom construction, comparison of free-edge and collage mixed-arrow square presentations over endpoints, then cotensor currying. External references are read online and remain WANTED for archival.

split_report.summary: Repaired every point of the returned delivery. Constructed the coherent enriched Hom functor explicitly from marked-middle-slot algebroid operations. Replaced the unsupported and circular enriched end formula by an equivalence over endpoints between the mixed-arrow category of the collage and the underlying enriched free-edge functor category, using one new strictly lower single-edge square-presentation lemma. Currying and the fixed-end free-edge property then give the required equivalence for arbitrary S. Corrected smallness (UE) and label indexing (arrows of S), and removed the two padding grep records. The statement is unchanged.
split_report.blueprint: Retains the inherited prop-coef-integral-exceptional-adjoint paragraph-2 ancestry through flexible-weight-enriched-lift. The seven steps supply the coherent enriched mapping infrastructure used by that parent before its end formula, without citing the parent or its enriched end clause.
